cards.q: Where does every C program start running?
cards.a:
In the function main

The operating system calls main.

cards.q: What does #include <stdio.h> do?
cards.a:
It inserts the declarations of functions like printf

Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces the line with the header's contents: the declarations of the standard input/output functions.

cards.q: What does return 0; at the end of main tell the operating system?
cards.a:
The program finished successfully

0 means success; other values mean an error.

cards.q: Which step joins your code with the code of printf?
cards.a:
Linking

printf's machine code lives in the C standard library; the linker joins them.

cards.q: How many bytes is an int on today's desktop computers?
cards.a:
4

C only promises at least 16 bits, but every mainstream platform today uses 32.

cards.q: What is in a local variable before you give it a value?
cards.a:
Whatever bits were already in that memory

The value is indeterminate, and reading it is a bug. Always initialise when you declare.

cards.q: What does printf("%d", 'A') print?
cards.a:
65

A char is a small number; %d prints it as a number.

cards.q: Which type should you normally use for numbers with a fraction?
cards.a:
double

double has about 15 significant digits; float only about 7.

cards.q: Which specifier prints a double with exactly 3 decimals?
cards.a:
%.3f

The precision goes after a dot.

cards.q: Why does scanf("%d", &n) need the &?
cards.a:
scanf needs n's address to store into it

Without `&`, scanf gets n's (garbage) value instead of where n lives, so it cannot store the number.

cards.q: What does scanf return if the user types "abc" for %d?
cards.a:
0: it read no values

Always check the return value.

cards.q: Which scanf specifier reads a double?
cards.a:
%lf

In scanf, %f is for float and %lf for double. In printf, %f prints both.

cards.q: What is 7 / 2 in C when both are ints?
cards.a:
3

Integer division throws the fraction away.

cards.q: How do you get 3.5 from int a = 7 and int b = 2?
cards.a:
(double)a / b

Convert before dividing. (double)(a / b) converts 3 to 3.0.

cards.q: What is 25 % 7?
What happens when a signed int overflows?
cards.a:
It is undefined behaviour: the language makes no promise

Unsigned types wrap predictably; signed overflow is a bug.

cards.q: What does printf("%d", 5 > 3) print?
cards.a:
1

Comparisons give 1 for true and 0 for false.

cards.q: Why does if (x = 5) always run its body?
cards.a:
It assigns 5 to x, and 5 counts as true

Use == to compare. The compiler warns about this with -Wall.

cards.q: In count != 0 && sum / count > 2, what happens when count is 0?
cards.a:
The division never runs, because && stops at the first false

Short-circuit evaluation.

cards.q: What happens if a case in a switch has no break?
cards.a:
Execution falls through into the next case's code

Sometimes intended, often a bug.

cards.q: How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) run?
What is special about do-while?
cards.a:
The body always runs at least once

The condition is checked after the body.

cards.q: What does continue do inside a for loop?
cards.a:
Skips to the step part and the next round

`continue` skips the rest of the body; the step (such as `i++`) still runs. `break` is what leaves the loop.

cards.q: What does scanf return when the input has ended?
cards.a:
EOF, a negative number

That is why loops test scanf(...) == 1.

cards.q: A function sets its parameter n = 0. What happens to the caller's variable?
cards.a:
Nothing: the parameter is a copy

C passes arguments by value.

cards.q: What is a prototype?
cards.a:
A declaration: the function's first line plus `;`

A prototype declares the function before its body, so you can call a function defined further down or in another file.

cards.q: What does void mean as a return type?
cards.a:
The function returns no value

Use plain return; to leave early.

cards.q: Where do a function's local variables live?
cards.a:
In its stack frame, released when it returns

Each call has its own frame.

cards.q: What does an uninitialised local int contain?
cards.a:
Garbage: whatever was in that memory

Locals are not cleared. Globals and statics start at 0.

cards.q: A function has static int calls = 0; calls++; return calls;. What does the third call return?
cards.a:
3

The static local keeps its value between calls.

cards.q: What does static mean on a function defined outside main?
cards.a:
It can only be called from code in the same file

On globals and functions, static means file-private.

cards.q: Where can a variable declared in a for statement be used?
cards.a:
Only inside that loop

Its scope is the loop.

cards.q: What is the last valid index of int a[8]?
cards.a:
7

Indexes go from 0 to length - 1.

cards.q: What happens when a program writes to a[20] in int a[8]?
cards.a:
It overwrites some other memory: anything can happen

C does not check indexes.

cards.q: Why does a function taking an array also need its length?
cards.a:
It only receives the address of the first element

Pass the count as a separate parameter.

cards.q: int a[10] = {0}; - what are the values?
cards.a:
All ten are 0

Missing initialisers are filled with 0.

cards.q: How many bytes does the string "dog" take?
cards.a:
4

Three characters and the '\0'.

cards.q: How do string functions know where a string ends?
cards.a:
They stop at the zero byte '\0'

The terminator is the only marker.

cards.q: What does a == b compare for two char arrays?
cards.a:
Their addresses

Use strcmp to compare the text.

cards.q: What does fgets leave at the end of the line it read?
cards.a:
The new line character, if it fitted, then '\0'

Remove it with buffer[strcspn(buffer, "\n")] = '\0';

cards.q: What does strcmp("cat", "cat") return?
cards.a:
0

0 means equal. Write strcmp(a, b) == 0.

cards.q: Why is snprintf safer than strcpy and strcat?
cards.a:
It is told the buffer size and never writes past it

It also always adds the terminator.

cards.q: What does strlen("hello") return?
cards.a:
5

The terminator is not counted.

cards.q: strchr("a=b", '=') returns...
cards.a:
A pointer to the '=' inside the string

`strchr` returns a pointer into the string, or NULL when the character is not there.

cards.q: int x = 5; int *p = &x; *p = 9; - what is x now?
cards.a:
9

*p is x itself.

cards.q: What does & give?
cards.a:
The address of a variable

& on one value (unary) is "address of". Between two values it is bitwise AND.

cards.q: What happens when a program dereferences NULL?
cards.a:
It usually crashes with a segmentation fault

Dereferencing NULL is undefined behaviour, and on normal systems it crashes. Always check pointers that might be NULL.

cards.q: How big is a char * on a 64-bit machine?
cards.a:
8 bytes, like every other pointer

A pointer holds an address, and every address is the same size.

cards.q: If p points at an int at address 1000, what address is p + 1?
cards.a:
1004

Pointer arithmetic moves by whole elements, and an int is 4 bytes.

cards.q: Which is the same as values[3]?
cards.a:
*(values + 3)

*values + 3 is the first element plus 3.

cards.q: Two pointers into the same array, q - p, gives...
cards.a:
The number of elements between them

The difference is in elements, like the addition.

cards.q: Can a pointer point one past the end of an array?
cards.a:
Yes, as long as it is never dereferenced

It is the usual "end" marker for loops.

cards.q: Why does scanf need &n rather than n?
cards.a:
To store into n, it needs n's address

Without the address, scanf would only get a copy of n's value.

cards.q: swap(int *a, int *b) is called as swap(&x, &y). Inside, what is *a?
cards.a:
x itself

a is the address; *a is the variable at that address.

cards.q: What is wrong with returning the address of a local variable?
cards.a:
The local stops existing when the function returns

It leaves a dangling pointer.

cards.q: How do functions usually report whether an out-parameter was filled?
cards.a:
Through their return value, such as true or false

Like `divide` above, or scanf's count of items read.

cards.q: With const int *p, which is allowed?
cards.a:
p = &other;

The int is read-only; the pointer can move.

cards.q: With int *const p, which is allowed?
cards.a:
*p = 5;

The pointer is fixed; the int can change.

cards.q: Why should size_t length(const char *s) take a const pointer?
cards.a:
It promises not to write, so literals can be passed

The function only reads, and `const` is a promise the compiler checks. It can then be called with string literals and other read-only text.

cards.q: Is passing an int * to a const int * parameter allowed?
cards.a:
Yes, automatically

Adding const is always safe; removing it is not.

cards.q: int **pp = &p; where p points at x. What is **pp?
cards.a:
x

Follow pp to p, then p to x.

cards.q: Why does a function take char **cursor instead of char *cursor?
cards.a:
So it can move the caller's pointer

The same reason swap takes int *.

cards.q: With ./tool one two, what is argc?
cards.a:
3

argv[0] is the program's name.

cards.q: const char *names[] = {"a", "bb"}; - what does the array hold?
cards.a:
Two pointers to text stored elsewhere

An array of strings is an array of pointers.

cards.q: When is heap memory released?
cards.a:
When the program calls free on it (or the program ends)

C has no garbage collector.

cards.q: What does malloc return when it cannot allocate?
cards.a:
NULL

Always check.

cards.q: Why is int *p = malloc(n * sizeof *p) a good pattern?
cards.a:
The size follows the pointer's type automatically

Change int to long and the allocation is still right.

cards.q: What is a memory leak?
cards.a:
Allocated memory that is never freed

The memory stays taken until the program exits.

cards.q: What can realloc do when the block cannot grow where it is?
cards.a:
Allocate a new block, copy the data and free the old one

That is why old pointers into the block become invalid.

cards.q: Why is p = realloc(p, n) a bug?
cards.a:
If realloc fails, the only pointer to the old block is lost

Use a temporary variable.

cards.q: Why does a growing array double its capacity instead of adding one?
cards.a:
So copying is rare and adding is fast on average

Doubling gives amortised constant-time adds; growing by one would copy everything on every add.

cards.q: What do length and capacity mean?
cards.a:
Elements in use, and elements there is room for

When length reaches capacity, grow.

cards.q: What does p->score mean when p is a struct pointer?
cards.a:
(*p).score

The arrow follows the pointer and picks the field.

cards.q: What happens when one struct variable is assigned to another?
cards.a:
Every field is copied, arrays inside included

Structs are values.

cards.q: Why can sizeof(struct) be bigger than the sum of its fields?
cards.a:
Padding is added to keep fields aligned

Reordering fields can reduce it.

cards.q: How do you compare two structs?
cards.a:
Field by field

C has no == for structs.

cards.q: What does typedef struct { int x; } Point; let you write?
cards.a:
Point p; instead of struct ... p;

typedef only adds a name.

cards.q: enum color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }; - what is BLUE?
cards.a:
2

Counting starts at 0.

cards.q: How big is a union of an int, a double and a char[3]?
cards.a:
The size of the double: the biggest member

All members share the same memory.

cards.q: What is the enum in a tagged union for?
cards.a:
Saying which member currently holds the value

Without it you cannot tell what is stored.

cards.q: How does the last node of a linked list mark the end?
cards.a:
Its next pointer is NULL

Loops stop when they reach NULL.

cards.q: Why does push_front take struct node **head?
cards.a:
It must change the caller's head pointer

The same idea as swap(int *, int *).

cards.q: In free_list, why save head->next before calling free(head)?
cards.a:
After free, reading head->next is a use after free

Freed memory is no longer yours.

cards.q: Which is faster on a linked list than on an array?
cards.a:
Inserting at the front

Arrays win at access by index and at walking through memory.

cards.q: Why are memory bugs in C dangerous even when the program seems to work?
cards.a:
They silently touch other memory, with effects later

The bad access reads or changes memory that belongs to something else, and the effects show up later or elsewhere. That is why tools are needed to find them.

cards.q: What does AddressSanitizer do?
cards.a:
Checks memory accesses and reports bad ones

It adds checks to every memory access and reports the first bad one with its line. Turn on Memory checks in the editor's menu.

cards.q: Which function should never be used to read a line?
cards.a:
gets

gets cannot know the buffer size. It was removed in C11.

cards.q: Which tool checks an unchanged program for leaks on Linux?
cards.a:
Valgrind

ASan needs a rebuild; Valgrind does not.

cards.q: What is 12 & 10?
How do you clear bit 2 of x?
cards.a:
x &= ~(1u << 2);

AND with a mask that has a 0 in that position only.

cards.q: What is 1u << 4?
cards.a:
16

Shifting left by n multiplies by 2 to the n.

cards.q: (0xABCD >> 8) & 0xFF gives...
cards.a:
0xAB

Shift the byte you want to the bottom, then mask.

cards.q: Which type is exactly 16 bits and unsigned?
cards.a:
uint16_t

short is usually 16 bits, but only uint16_t promises it.

cards.q: On a little-endian computer, which byte of 0x11223344 is stored first?
cards.a:
0x44

The least significant byte comes first.

cards.q: Why build a file's bytes with shifts rather than writing a uint32_t's memory directly?
cards.a:
Shifts give the same byte order on every machine

The value, not the memory layout, decides the bytes.

cards.q: What does "%" PRIu64 do?
cards.a:
Gives the right printf format for uint64_t

The macro expands to a string like "lu" or "llu", whichever this system needs.

cards.q: What does fopen("log.txt", "w") do to an existing log.txt?
cards.a:
Empties it

Use "a" to add to the end instead.

cards.q: How do you find out why fopen failed?
cards.a:
errno, through perror or strerror

fopen returns NULL and sets errno.

cards.q: fread(buffer, 4, 10, f) returns 7. What happened?
cards.a:
Only 7 items of 4 bytes could be read

The count is in items, not bytes. Fewer than asked usually means the end of the file (or an error, which `ferror` tells apart).

cards.q: Why write errors to stderr instead of stdout?
cards.a:
They stay visible when output is redirected

Results and messages go to different places, so `prog > out.txt` still shows errors on the terminal.

cards.q: #define DOUBLE(x) x + x. What is 3 * DOUBLE(2)?
cards.a:
8

It becomes 3 * 2 + 2. Parenthesise the body.

cards.q: What does an include guard prevent?
cards.a:
A header's contents appearing twice when it is included twice

#ifndef NAME / #define NAME / ... / #endif.

cards.q: Why is MAX(i++, j) risky with #define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))?
cards.a:
i++ may run twice

Macro arguments are pasted wherever the parameter appears.

cards.q: When does the preprocessor run?
cards.a:
Before the compiler, on the source text

It only edits text.

cards.q: What belongs in a header file?
cards.a:
Declarations: types, prototypes, extern variables

Definitions go in the .c file; a header that defines things causes duplicate definitions when two files include it.

cards.q: "undefined reference to foo" comes from...
cards.a:
The linker: foo was never defined

The code compiled fine because foo was declared, but nothing linked in defines it, so the pieces did not join up.

cards.q: How should a global variable be shared between files?
cards.a:
`extern` in the header, one definition in a .c file

Defining it in the header gives a definition in every file that includes it; `static` would give each file its own variable.

cards.q: What does make do?
cards.a:
It rebuilds only what changed

make follows the dependencies listed in the Makefile and compares file times, rebuilding only targets older than their sources.

cards.q: What is int (*f)(double)?
cards.a:
A pointer to a function taking a double and returning an int

The parentheses around *f make it a pointer.

cards.q: What must a qsort comparison function return?
cards.a:
Negative, zero or positive

The sign says the order of the two elements, like strcmp.

cards.q: Why does qsort take void pointers?
cards.a:
To sort arrays of any element type

The element size is given separately, and the comparison function knows the real type.

cards.q: Why is return a - b; a risky comparison?
cards.a:
The subtraction can overflow for large values

Compare with < and > instead.

cards.q: What may a program with undefined behaviour do?
cards.a:
Anything, including appearing to work

The standard places no requirements on it, so the program may work today and fail with another compiler or flag.

cards.q: Why can x + 1 < x be replaced by 0?
cards.a:
The compiler may assume signed overflow never happens

It optimises on that assumption.

cards.q: Which of these is defined behaviour?
cards.a:
UINT_MAX + 1u, which is 0

Unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition.

cards.q: How do you safely test whether a + b would overflow for positive b?
cards.a:
if (a > INT_MAX - b) before adding

The other two tests rely on the overflow having happened.

cards.q: Where does the first int argument arrive on x86-64 Linux?
cards.a:
In edi (the low half of rdi)

Then rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9.

cards.q: What does values[i] become for an int array?
cards.a:
A memory access at values + i * 4

[rdi+rdx*4] in Intel syntax.

cards.q: How does an if statement appear in assembly?
cards.a:
A comparison that sets flags, then a conditional jump

The processor has jumps, not structured statements.

cards.q: What does inlining mean?
cards.a:
Copying a function's body in place of the call

Inlining removes the call, which saves its cost and opens more optimisations.

cards.q: Which function copies memory correctly when the source and destination overlap?
cards.a:
memmove

memcpy is allowed to assume they do not overlap.

cards.q: What does srand(42) followed by rand() calls give in every run?
cards.a:
The same sequence of numbers

Seed with time(NULL) for different runs.

cards.q: Is rand() suitable for making passwords?
cards.a:
No: its sequence is predictable

Use the operating system's secure random generator for anything secret.

cards.q: How does a variadic function know how many arguments it was given?
cards.a:
The caller tells it, such as with a count

stdarg.h gives no way to ask; the caller passes a count, a sentinel or a format string.

cards.q: What is a collision in a hash table?
cards.a:
Two different keys landing in the same bucket

Chaining keeps both in that bucket's list.

cards.q: What is the load factor?
cards.a:
Entries divided by buckets

Keep it low by growing the table.

cards.q: Why must a hash table store its own copy of each key string?
cards.a:
The caller may reuse its buffer later

The caller's buffer may be changed or reused after inserting, so the table keeps its own copy, and must then free those copies.

cards.q: Why use unsigned arithmetic inside a hash function?
cards.a:
Unsigned overflow wraps around and is well defined

Signed overflow would be undefined behaviour.

cards.q: Why can a variadic function not find out how many arguments it received?
cards.a:
C passes no count or type information, so it must be told by a count, a sentinel or a format

Nothing is passed besides the values themselves. `printf` knows how many to read from its format string; other functions take a count or stop at a sentinel such as NULL.

cards.q: What type should `va_arg` use for an argument that was passed as a `float`?
cards.a:
`double`, because floats are promoted to double when passed through `...`

Default argument promotions turn a float into a double, and char and short into int. Reading it with `va_arg(ap, float)` is undefined behaviour.

cards.q: You need to walk the same va_list twice. What do you use?
cards.a:
va_copy to make a second list

va_copy makes an independent copy that can be walked separately; each needs its own va_end.

cards.q: Why is `struct { char a; double b; char c; }` bigger than 10 bytes?
cards.a:
Padding keeps `b` and arrays of it aligned

`b` must start at a multiple of 8, and the size is rounded up to the struct's alignment: on a typical 64-bit system 1 + 7 padding + 8 + 1 + 7 = 24 bytes. Ordering the members largest first shrinks it to 16.
cards.lessonTitle: Struct Layout, Alignment and Bit Fields

cards.q: Why are bit fields a poor choice for a file format?
cards.a:
Their layout is up to each compiler

The order and packing of the bits are implementation-defined, so another compiler may read them differently. Use shifts and masks on fixed-width integers.
cards.lessonTitle: Struct Layout, Alignment and Bit Fields

cards.q: Where must a flexible array member go?
cards.a:
last in the struct

It has no fixed size, so nothing can come after it.
cards.lessonTitle: Struct Layout, Alignment and Bit Fields

cards.q: In `int a[6] = { [4] = 9 };`, what are the other elements?
cards.a:
0

Elements not mentioned in an initializer are set to zero, even inside a function. Only an array with no initializer at all is left indeterminate.

cards.q: When is a `_Static_assert` checked?
cards.a:
While compiling: a false condition stops the build with its message

`_Static_assert` tests a constant expression at compile time. `assert` is the run-time check that `NDEBUG` turns off.

cards.q: What does _Generic((x), int: "i", double: "d", default: "?") give when x is a float?
cards.a:
"?"

_Generic matches the exact type; float is neither int nor double, so default is used.

cards.q: Why copy `errno` straight after the failing call?
cards.a:
The next library call, even a successful one like `printf`, may change it

Library functions may set `errno` even when they succeed, so save it in a local before calling anything else.

cards.q: Why are the cleanup labels in reverse order of acquiring?
cards.a:
A jump frees exactly what was acquired so far

Each label frees one resource and falls into the next. A failure at step N jumps to the label for step N − 1, so exactly the earlier resources are freed, newest first.

cards.q: Which should never be checked with assert?
cards.a:
whether malloc returned NULL

malloc can fail in a correct program, and assert disappears with NDEBUG: it needs real handling.

cards.q: Why does giving each thread its own result slot avoid locking?
cards.a:
No two threads write the same memory, so there is no data race

Races need two threads touching the same memory with at least one writing. The main thread reads the slots only after `thrd_join`, which orders it after the writes.

cards.q: Why must `cnd_wait` be called in a loop?
cards.a:
A thread can wake without the condition being true, so it must check again

Wake-ups can be spurious, or another thread may have taken the item first. `while (!ready) cnd_wait(&cv, &m);` checks again each time.

cards.q: Several threads only need to increase one shared counter. What is simplest?
cards.a:
an atomic counter with atomic_fetch_add

One atomic operation per increase is indivisible: no lock needed and no updates lost.

cards.q: What does `snprintf(NULL, 0, fmt, ...)` return?
cards.a:
The length the full output would have

With size 0 nothing is written, but the return value (not counting the terminating zero) tells you how big a buffer to allocate; add 1 for the zero.

cards.q: Why does the capacity double instead of growing by the amount needed?
cards.a:
So reallocations stay rare and appending is O(1) on average

Growing by exactly what is needed copies the whole string on every append, O(n²) in total. Doubling uses some extra memory but copies far less.

cards.q: Why is strcat in a loop slow for long strings?
cards.a:
It searches for the end of the string each time

strcat has to find the terminating zero first, so each append costs the current length; keeping the length yourself avoids the scan.

cards.q: Why cast a `void *` to `unsigned char *` before adding an offset?
cards.a:
Pointer arithmetic needs a pointed-to size, and `unsigned char` is one byte, so the offset counts bytes

Standard C does not allow arithmetic on `void *`, because `void` has no size. Through `unsigned char *`, `p + i * size` moves exactly that many bytes.

cards.q: What must be true of an array before `bsearch` can search it?
cards.a:
It must be sorted with the same comparison

Binary search relies on the order. If the array is sorted another way than the comparison given to `bsearch`, it can miss elements that are there.

cards.q: A comparison function for qsort on ints returns a - b. What can go wrong?
cards.a:
It can overflow and give the wrong sign

For values far apart, such as INT_MAX and -1, signed overflow is undefined and can flip the sign; `(a > b) - (a < b)` is always safe.

cards.q: What does `t.tm_mon == 0` mean?
cards.a:
January

Months in `struct tm` count from 0, so January is 0 and December is 11. Days of the month (`tm_mday`) start at 1.

cards.q: How can `mktime` help with "30 days after this date"?
cards.a:
Add 30 to `tm_mday` and call `mktime`; it normalises the date into the right month and year

`mktime` accepts out-of-range fields and fixes them up, so day 45 of a month becomes the right day of the next month, across years too.

cards.q: Which gives the time as text in ISO 8601 form?
cards.a:
`strftime(buf, sizeof buf, "%FT%T", t)`

strftime does the formatting; `%F` is `%Y-%m-%d` and `%T` is `%H:%M:%S`. printf does not understand `%Y`, and asctime and ctime use their own fixed layout.

cards.q: Why should error messages go to `stderr`?
cards.a:
So redirected output holds only the real results

`prog > out.txt` captures `stdout` only. Messages on `stderr` still reach the person on the terminal and do not mix with the data.

cards.q: What does `--` on a command line mean?
cards.a:
The end of the options

Everything after `--` is an argument even if it starts with `-`, so `-notes.txt` is taken as a file name.

cards.q: A tool finished but one of its three input files was missing. What exit code fits the conventions?
cards.a:
A non-zero code such as 1

Any failure should give a non-zero code, after printing the problem to stderr, so scripts can notice it.

cards.q: Why is `if (a + b < a)` a broken overflow test for `int`?
cards.a:
The overflow is undefined, so the test may be removed

The overflow has already happened, and because signed overflow is undefined the compiler may assume `a + b < a` is false for positive b. Check before adding: `b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b`.

cards.q: What happens to `-1` in `strlen(s) > -1`?
cards.a:
It is converted to `size_t`, becoming the largest value, so the comparison is always false

In a comparison with a `size_t`, -1 is converted to unsigned and becomes `SIZE_MAX`. The compiler may warn, but it accepts the code.

cards.q: Which is a safe check before computing a * b for size_t values?
cards.a:
if (a != 0 && b > SIZE_MAX / a)

Dividing the limit by one factor tells whether the other fits, without overflowing first.

cards.q: Why does `rand() % n` favour small numbers?
cards.a:
The values past the last multiple of n wrap onto small ones

`rand` is uniform, but when `RAND_MAX + 1` is not a multiple of n, the last incomplete group maps only onto 0, 1, 2 and so on, giving those results an extra chance.

cards.q: Why keep a generator's state in a struct instead of a global?
cards.a:
Each user gets its own repeatable stream

With one global state, any other caller changes the sequence you get. A state struct per part of the program, or per thread, keeps runs repeatable and safe across threads.

cards.q: In Fisher-Yates, element i - 1 is swapped with...
cards.a:
a random position from 0 to i - 1

Choosing only among positions not yet fixed is what makes every order equally likely.
